Old post 2:
Over the past year, I’ve noticed how prominently “reasoning” features in AI marketing and research proposals.

It’s often framed as a breakthrough — as if models have crossed a cognitive threshold. As if they suddenly learned to 𝑡ℎ𝑖𝑛𝑘.

But what if they’re mostly just… counting on their fingers?

In my newest post, I argue that reasoning models are less magical than they seem. Consider this analogy:

A preschooler can do small additions:
3+3=6, 7+1=8.
Sometimes they slip: 4+5=8.

If you guide them to count on their fingers before answering, accuracy improves. But that doesn’t mean they’ve developed a deeper understanding of mathematics. They’re just taking more careful intermediate steps.

Inference-time scaling works similarly.
More tokens → more steps → higher probability of landing on the correct answer.

The improvement is real. But it’s not necessarily a qualitative leap in cognition.

In the post, I break down:
• Why internal monologues are often statistical pattern reproduction
• What reasoning models are actually optimizing
• The hidden computational and economic costs of “letting them think”

If you're building with LLMs or evaluating reasoning-heavy systems, this perspective might help calibrate expectations.

🔗 Full post: https://lnkd.in/dzTk37XG

Happy to discuss — especially if you disagree!

Old post 3:
Tokenization is the first step in the processing chain of every large language model — and it’s more impactful than it sounds.

How we split raw text into discrete chunks determines sequence lengths, vocabulary sizes, and even how models generalize to words they’ve never seen. Getting this step right was a key factor in making modern LLMs so large and capable.

In my latest post, I explore the extremes of tokenization:

• Tiny tokens → enormous sequences, slower inference  
• Huge vocab → huge memory footprint, rare word problems  
• Subwords → the elegant balance that modern LLMs rely on

I break down why subword tokenization works from first principles, and how spaces, typos, and even emojis fit neatly into this puzzle.

📖 Read more in "From Text to Tokens: The Balancing Act Behind LLM Vocabularies"  
🔗 https://lnkd.in/dtRn5Yg2

Curious to hear your thoughts — have you noticed the quirks of subword tokenization in your own work?
